etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English plomme, ploume, from Old English plūme, from Proto-West Germanic *plūmā, borrowed from Latin prūnum. Doublet of prune.

definitions.definition: An edible, fleshy stone fruit of Prunus domestica (European plum), often of a dark red or purple colour. [from 8th c.]
A stone-fruit tree which bears this fruit, Prunus domestica. [from 8th c.]
Prunus cerasifera (cherry plum or myrobalan)
Prunus salicina (Chinese plum or Japanese plum)
Prunus spinosa (sloe)
Prunus ursina (bear's plum)
Prunus sect. Prunus
Prunus americana (American plum)
Prunus angustifolia (Chickasaw plum or sand plum)
Prunus hortulana (hortulan plum)
Prunus nigra (Canadian plum or black plum)
Prunus rivularis (creek plum or hog plum)
Prunus subcordata (Klamath plum or Oregon plum)
Prunus sect. Prunocerasus North American plums
Prunus mume, an Asian fruit more closely related to the apricot than the plum, usually consumed pickled, dried, or as a juice or wine; ume.
Prunus sect. Armeniaca (better known as apricots)
The edible, fleshy stone fruit of several species resembling the plum, or the tree from which they grow. [from 16th c.]
(now rare) A dried grape or raisin, as used in a pudding or cake. [from 17th c.]

quote.citation: 1870, Louisa May Alcott, An Old-Fashioned Girl:
quote.text: “Bright boy! here’s a plum for you,” and Polly threw a plump raisin into his mouth.
Little Jack Horner sat in a corner, eating a Christmas pie; he put in his thumb, and he took out a plum, and said, “What a good boy am I!”

definitions.definition: The fruit and its tree.
(now rare, archaic) One hundred thousand pounds; (generally) a fortune. [from 18th c.]

quote.citation: 1751, [Tobias] Smollett, The Adventures of Peregrine Pickle […], volume (please specify |volume=I to IV), London: Harrison and Co., […], →OCLC:
quote.text: He  […]  acquired a plentiful fortune, tho', to his infinite regret, he died before it amounted to a Plum  […] .

definitions.definition: A desirable or choice thing of its kind; a prize selection; a choice appointment, assignment etc. [from 19th c.]

quote.citation: 1880, William Blades, The Enemies of Books, page 52:
quote.text: Such chances as this do not fall to a man's lot twice; but Edmond Werdet relates a story very similar indeed, and where also the "plums" fell into the lap of a London dealer.

quote.citation: 1980 December 13, Ronnie Allen, “Anita's Latest”, in Gay Community News, volume 8, number 21, page 5:
quote.text: As to Rev. Jerry [Falwell], he, of course, is "not anti-homosexual" but "anti-homosexuality." I guess that's his same bit of down home sophistry that explains that God listens to the prayers of Jews, if they are consciously praying to a Christian God, one of the Rev.'s latest dialectic plums.

definitions.definition: A dark bluish-red color/colour, the colour of some plums. [from 19th c.]
(vulgar, slang, usually in the plural) A testicle. [from 20th c.]
(derogatory, chiefly UK) A fool, an idiot.
Extended senses.
(comparable) Of a dark bluish-red colour.
(not comparable) Choice; especially lavish or preferred.

quote.citation: 1960 March, G. Freeman Allen, “Europe's most luxurious express - the "Settebello"”, in Trains Illustrated, page 146:
quote.text: It is obviously a "plum" job, one distinction being that its motormen are granted an allowance of about 6s. [six shillings] towards the cost of Wagons-Lits food in the crew quarters of the train, [...]. Additionally, by the way, each man is allowed a quarter of a bottle of wine "on the house" per trip!

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Phonetically based spelling of plumb.

definitions.definition: Plumb
Completely; utterly.
(mining) To plumb.
